Understanding how motivation shapes students’ engagement with laboratory skill development is critical for effective learning and academic achievement. Physical science laboratories function as experiential learning environments that support the development of advanced conceptual understanding and procedural competence; students’ attitudes toward these environments influence the efficacy of skill training. During the COVID-19 pandemic, computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) emerged as viable alternatives for skill instruction and experimentation under lockdown constraints. However, widespread adoption of VLs has been hindered by limited awareness and familiarity among both teachers and students.

This study investigated the motivational determinants of VL effectiveness for teaching laboratory skills and procedures. Data were collected using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), self-reported measures of extrinsic motivation, and a teacher perception scale specific to VLs. Independent-samples t tests and automatic linear modeling (ALM) were employed to analyze the data. The findings indicate that animated, graphics-rich instructional materials in VLs elicited higher levels of intrinsic motivation among students than e-book–based materials. Teacher engagement also played a significant role in enhancing students’ motivation to conduct experiments in VLs. Furthermore, extended or repeated engagement with VL experiments was positively associated with improvements in students’ laboratory performance.

These results underscore the importance of instructional design and teacher facilitation in maximizing the pedagogical value of VLs and suggest that sustained, iterative practice within VL environments can strengthen laboratory competencies.
